## Changed

- `structured` markdown reads tables from the page's drawing. A browser-printed
  HTML table or a typeset use table is the grid its rules draw; every character
  is placed in the cell its centre falls in, merged cells are read from missing
  rules, and a header block repeated with other column widths becomes its own
  table. Rows of filled chips with no rules are a table too, and when a table's
  cells carry two or more colours each value is followed by its colour's name
  (`R-1 [green]`). A framed text box is its own block. Only `markdown` changes:
  `spans` and the `complex_table` routing flag are computed exactly as in 0.17.
- `structured` markdown keeps list markers as printed (`1.`, `a.`, `(2)`, `iv.`)
  and indents nested items, instead of replacing every marker with `- `. In an
  ordinance the marker is the provision's address.
- `structured` markdown reads page columns that share baselines, and a heading
  printed to the left of the text it heads, as columns; lines of sentences that
  happen to line up are no longer taken for a table.
- Text outside the page box is left out of `structured` markdown.

Measured on `data/text` (14 pages of zoning codes and plans from five cities,
each graded against a ledger of what the page prints; six of the pages were
held out while the rules were written): 413 of 413 facts, against 97 for 0.17,
336 for `pdftotext -layout` and 318 for the Docling server. The per-page table
is produced by `scripts/text-bench.py`; `tests/text_ledgers.rs` keeps the
toolkit at full marks.
